title: What film, in your opinion, has the most natural/realistic acting and dialogue?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]
[removed]

Have a look Autumn Sonata. The scene between Ingrid Bergman and Liv Ullman when they telling each other some truths.  It is the best acted scene ever in my eyes.  I needed to take a breath after I saw it for the first time.
[removed]

Recently watched McCabe & Mrs. Miller so my mind instantly goes there. Altman is known for his purposefully messy dialogue but the way people step on each other's lines in this film is absolutely wild. In crowd scenes without subtitles you literally just have to follow the mood of the scene because no individual party is consistently audible. It's great naturalistic dialogue too, tons of half-formed statements, non sequiturs, characters repeating themselves or talking past each other. Fantastic movie.

As far as genre movies, The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973) is beautifully realistic, and it doesn't sacrifice entertainment for realism. It gets down to the nitty gritty of the early 70's Boston crime underworld, and it focuses on peripheral figures.

It's a largely hated subgenre but when it comes to dialogue I think mumblecore has some of the best examples. "Funny Ha Ha" is painful for some but for it's a radical exercise on realism and awkwardness.

Outside of mumblecore, I think Bergman's Scenes from a Marriage really feels true to life.

The French Connection is one of my favorite movies so I give it as an example. Especially, considering it was made in 1971. Many New Hollywood movies are the same, think of All the President's Men. 

Of more recent ones, I think of what the Safdie Brothers are doing these days. I think what is called indie movies, if not deliberately stylized then they have a more natural acting/talking style.
[removed]
[removed]

In the Name of the Father comes to mind. Daniel Day Lewis and Pete Postlethwaite have some truly wonderful scenes together in prison, as they tried to patch up their broken relationship after a huge tragedy and led them there. Between the acting and dialog, it really felt like a father and son trying to figure out where things went wrong.

Weird and obscure pick maybe, but [Wendigo (2001)](https://letterboxd.com/film/wendigo/). Terribly underrated. Wrings a potent atmosphere out of its setting and shoestring budget. Remarkably believable performances and dialogue. Creative editing. Interesting juxtaposition of folk-horror myth and what frightens us in the real world.
This, 100%!

The one that's really stood out to me recently is How To Have Sex. All the performances are incredibly natural and realistic, and it's got some of the most realistic scenes of people being very drunk I've ever seen. Everything about the film rings true.
[removed]
[removed]

Napoleon Dynamite.

Not for the acting ( which is kind of campy) but humans in real life tend to say a lot of illogical and non-prosey things.  

As much as I like the dramatized way that humans can speak in movies ( The Princess Bride is infinitely quotable!) I believe that real life is more awkward, oddly inappropriate ( usually to subject matter, not in a lewd way)  and usually vapid, not going to lie. 

* excerpt--

Napoleon ( to the chicken farmer) - do the chickens have large Talons?

Farmer- do they have what?

Napoleon - Large _talons.

Farmer I don't understand a word you just said.

____

Now what could be at play is either the farmer is extremely hard of hearing which is highly possible or he's ashamed that he doesn't know what the word "Talons" (bird claws) means but whatever the case it isn't this dramatized," I say witty thing, you say witty thing"  that most screenplays, good or bad, tend to 
..implement.
[removed]

The central performance of Oslo, August 31st is astonishing and feels true to life. The scene between the main character and his old friend is so moving, starting with male bravado before ultimately moving to something much more moving and honest.
[removed]
Campy by design tho naturally
Agree. I really love Funny Ha Ha. Andrew Bujalski also makes some great films with very realistic dialogue.
[removed]
1970s in general was great for naturalistic dialogue. Even Rocky can feel like a documentary at times.

Wouldn’t call it the most since it’s a bit of recency bias but I watched Tyler Perry’s Why Did I Get Married last night and I have to say I was incredibly impressed by the dialogue and acting performances. I thought it felt very natural to me compared to a lot of movies cut from the same cloth

I mean Where is the Friends house and a few other kierostomi flicks for sure bc of the use of non actors. Some of my favorite films are by him precisely because the acting is so natural it doesn’t even seem like acting.

"I wrote your stupid name in the ground and I pissed on it!"

Pissed right in the name of the father.

Bo Burnham's *Eighth Grade*

It's so realistic that it's almost like he went into an actual middle school to film real kids. There's a scene where they have a school shooter drill and one of the kids is talking about how of it was real he wouldn't be a pussy and he's elbow the shooter and take the gun. This 14 year old kid acting nonchalant tough like life is that easy. I can totally see actual middle school kids saying that exact thing

Anything that Shane Meadows has done but in particular I would say :

This is England 
Dead man’s shoes 

He relies heavily on improv and I think it really tells. I don’t know if anyone has watched the subsequent this is England series that came out on television but the standard of realistic dialogue is arguably even higher in those. Those of you that have watched the series will remember the table scene and the scene where Woody and Milky run into each other I’m sure. Incredible.

Yes.

The whole Koker trilogy.

I'd also add a film he wrote but did not direct, *The White Balloon*.

This is a great pick. The scene where the father and daughter are opening up to each other near the fire and she kind of struggles to find the words, and the scene in the car (which was awful and made my stomach drop) but that sense of ramped up discomfort slowly escalating into panic with the nervous laughter and her eventually blurting something out were particular stand outs for me in realistic exchanges.

Some that felt very real at least to me are The Florida Project, Lilja 4ever, And Here’s What’s Happening to Me (Со мною вот что происходит), The Practice of Beauty (Упражнения в прекрасном), The Fool (Дурак). Also many Baumbach movies feel pretty real, at least to me, like Frances Ha, Marriage Story, Meyerowitz Stories.

"Blue is the warmest color" had the most natural/realistic acting and dialogs I have seen in a movie.

Safdie's brothers movies also are quite realistic. "Heaven knows what" won an award for a documentary despite being a scripted movie.

"Dog Day Afternoon" is also worth checking.
3 Women is really natural too. Like just a hidden camera spying on these women from across the street.

I'd say anything directed by Cassavetes. Also, Mikey & Nicky. The way he lets his actors go free you really get a lot of naturalistic dialog. This is probably best seen in Husbands.
[removed]
Even though he doesn't say it I always do my Mitchum impression saying: Son of a bitch, I gotta have those gunnnns. In my deepest voice.

A Guide to Recognizing Your Saints is one of the first movies I saw where I felt like the characters cross-talked and talked over each other in a realistic way that impressed me. I know there's many more examples, but I don't see this one mentioned often and I think it excels in that area.
